subcomponents.title: Uses scene-kit APIs without bypassing or duplicating them

criteria.rationale: Talk.tsx renders the kit's Presentation with the presentation-owned steps, title and initialMode. It does not reimplement navigation, stage or chrome. steps.tsx builds typed Step objects (id, era, title, caption, payload, Scene, groupKey) from the kit's Step type. Stage.tsx, the shared boundary, renders step.Scene with payload, step and index inside the kit's LayoutGroup and AnimatePresence. EvolvingScene.tsx composes only kit nodes (SceneLayer, Box, SymbolChip, Arrow, Label, Emphasis, Frame) and the kit's SceneProps type. Every kit node wraps motion.div or motion.span with layout and layoutId, so the demo uses the kit's morph mechanism and does not duplicate it.

subcomponents.title: Uses stable identities and appropriate grouped-scene architecture

criteria.rationale: The nine steps are generated in one place, steps.tsx. A single outline.map gives every step Scene: EvolvingScene and groupKey 'sample-evolving-scene'. Stage.tsx turns that into sceneKey = `${groupKey}:${sceneIdentity(Scene)}` and uses it as the key of the motion.div canvas. Adjacent steps therefore keep the same key and the same Scene component, so the scene instance stays mounted and only the payload changes. A single shared groupKey is correct for this one continuously evolving scene. Entity identity is separate from groupKey. entities.ts defines entity(name) = 'how-to-make-a-presentation:'+name. EvolvingScene.tsx passes entity('you'), entity('skill'), entity('step-N'), entity('morph-N') and the other ids as layoutId to the kit nodes. Box, Arrow, SymbolChip, Label, Emphasis, Frame and SceneLayer forward layoutId to motion elements with layout, and Stage wraps them in a LayoutGroup. The ids are stable across steps, and entities that persist between steps keep the same id. For example, 'you' appears at every step and 'skill' from step 2 onward. Because the ids are stable, the kit's layout mechanism animates a persisting entity from its old state to its new one.
evidence: steps.tsx: groupKey 'sample-evolving-scene' on all nine mapped steps
Stage.tsx: sceneKey from groupKey plus sceneIdentity(step.Scene), used as the motion.div key
entities.ts: entity() helper
EvolvingScene.tsx: layoutId={entity(...)} on every node, including Arrow connectors
nodes/*.tsx: layout and layoutId forwarded to motion elements
judging basis: consensus-pass

subcomponents.title: Maintains clear boundaries and scope discipline

criteria.rationale: The shared kit exports a public constant, PRESENTATION_HOOKS, that nothing in the delivered source consumes, and its comment says the opposite. src/presentation-kit/constants.ts:18-23 declares it and says the hooks are consumed by verification, inspection and presentation CSS. A repo-wide search for the identifier finds only that declaration and the identical one in the bootstrap template copy. The only other reference is the `export * from './constants'` re-export in src/presentation-kit/index.ts, which uses no member. Every real consumer hard-codes the attribute strings instead. Footer.tsx, Toc.tsx, Header.tsx, Presentation.tsx, Stage.tsx and the node components write literals such as `data-presentation-active`. The presentation's talk.css, presentation.test.tsx and Appear.test.tsx use literal selectors. The result is a dead, misleading shared contract, which the guidance says to score once under this criterion even though the declaration is in the kit. The rest of the boundaries are sound. Talk.tsx passes the required title to Presentation, and Header.tsx renders it in browse mode, so the title input is consumed. The presentation-owned `entity()` helper is used for every layoutId in EvolvingScene.tsx. Those points do not offset the dead and misleading PRESENTATION_HOOKS contract.

subcomponents.title: Fixed-canvas uniform viewport fitting

criteria.rationale: `getFitScale` returns one factor, min(1, availW/880, availH/380), floored at MIN_SCALE. Stage applies it as `transform: scale(s)`, the same factor on both axes, to a fixed 880×380 canvas, so the internal composition doesn't reflow. The stage shell is `inset: 0` over the full viewport, so using window dimensions is consistent. At 1280×720 browse, availW is 1208 and availH is 530, giving scale 1. At 390×844 browse, availW is 318, giving 0.361 (above the 0.28 floor), so the canvas is 318px wide inside 390. Present mode uses less reserved space and also fits.

criteria.rationale: I agree with judges A and B. All four copies spawn Vite's own binary with process.execPath, not through an npm or npx wrapper. The child they track is therefore the preview server itself. In verify, the preview is created in renderRoutes, and readiness, chromium.launch, and every route check all sit inside one try whose finally runs `await browser?.close(); await stopPreview()`. stopPreview sends SIGTERM to the process group and awaits the child's 'exit' event, capped at 3s, and only then escalates to SIGKILL. Success, a failing check, a browser launch failure, and a later thrown error therefore all pass through the same awaited cleanup. The template copies are identical apart from the removed sample check, and the contract test enforces that. Judge C's reason does not decide the requirement. The SIGKILL without a second await is reached only when the server ignores SIGTERM for 2–3s. That is a hypothetical hang the candidate does not produce, not one of the named exit paths. On every named path the server is terminated and its exit awaited. The integration test also confirms that the port is refused after inspect exits.

subcomponents.title: Skill instructions and templates

criteria.rationale: No test materializes the presentation templates, so I traced them by hand. SKILL.md documents the destination as src/presentations/<slug>/, with templates/presentation/ copied there. From that destination, every relative import, CSS import, required prop and field name resolves against the bootstrapped layout and the kit's types. Imports: Talk.tsx imports '../../presentation-kit', which from src/presentations/<slug>/ is src/presentation-kit, inside src. Its other imports are ./steps/step and ./presentation.css, both copied alongside it, so the CSS import resolves. steps/ExampleScene.tsx and steps/step.tsx use '../../../presentation-kit' and '../../../presentation-kit/types'; from src/presentations/<slug>/steps/ these resolve to src/presentation-kit and src/presentation-kit/types, so none escapes src. The bootstrap barrel presentation-kit/index.ts exports ./Presentation, ./nodes/Label and ./nodes/SceneLayer, so Presentation, Label and SceneLayer all resolve. Props and fields: Step<TPayload> extends StepMeta (id, era, title, caption) and adds payload, Scene and optional groupKey, and the template step sets exactly those fields. ExampleScene is typed SceneProps<{label:string}>, which matches Scene<Payload>. Presentation requires steps and title, and Talk.tsx passes both plus the optional initialMode. Label and SceneLayer take NodeProps, whose props are all optional, and the template passes layoutId and children, which exist. The bootstrap tsconfig.app.json enables noUnusedLocals, noUnusedParameters and verbatimModuleSyntax; the templates use import type correctly and have no unused locals. entities.ts only exports entity, and <slug> appears only inside a string literal. The bootstrap's own starter presentation uses the same import shapes and field names against the same kit, and its registry entry imports './starter/Talk' correctly. The inspect template (bootstrap/scripts/inspect-presentation.mjs) imports only node built-ins and playwright, and it is not in the tsconfig include of src, so it has no relative imports to resolve. The remaining risk is that no test builds the presentation templates, but the trace finds no unmet clause.

votes.rationale: The nine steps are generated in one place, steps.tsx. A single outline.map gives every step Scene: EvolvingScene and groupKey 'sample-evolving-scene'. Stage.tsx turns that into sceneKey = `${groupKey}:${sceneIdentity(Scene)}` and uses it as the key of the motion.div canvas. Adjacent steps therefore keep the same key and the same Scene component, so the scene instance stays mounted and only the payload changes. A single shared groupKey is correct for this one continuously evolving scene. Entity identity is separate from groupKey. entities.ts defines entity(name) = 'how-to-make-a-presentation:'+name. EvolvingScene.tsx passes entity('you'), entity('skill'), entity('step-N'), entity('morph-N') and the other ids as layoutId to the kit nodes. Box, Arrow, SymbolChip, Label, Emphasis, Frame and SceneLayer forward layoutId to motion elements with layout, and Stage wraps them in a LayoutGroup. The ids are stable across steps, and entities that persist between steps keep the same id. For example, 'you' appears at every step and 'skill' from step 2 onward. Because the ids are stable, the kit's layout mechanism animates a persisting entity from its old state to its new one.

votes.rationale: Grouping: `steps.tsx` builds all nine steps from one outline map with `Scene: EvolvingScene` and `groupKey: 'sample-evolving-scene'`. `Stage` computes `sceneKey = groupKey:sceneIdentity(step.Scene)`, which is identical for every step. The single keyed `motion.div` inside `AnimatePresence` therefore stays mounted, and each step only passes a new `payload`/`index` to the same `SceneComponent`. The nine steps are generated by one map, so there is no per-step module to check. Identity: the presentation-owned `entity(name)` helper in `entities.ts` creates stable ids. `EvolvingScene` passes them as `layoutId` on every rendered node: you, prompt, skill, conversation, question, step-N, morph-N, ghost, verify, depth, kit-link, kit, modify, edited and reveal. votes.rationale: Readiness comes from HTTP polling of `http://127.0.0.1:${port}/`, not from the child's own announcement of its address. The only ownership check is `previewAlive(child)`, sampled at the top of each polling iteration, so the child's exit is not raced against readiness. A stale server on the port (for instance one bound after freePort releases it, or a user-supplied --port) can answer the fetch before the child's exit is observed. `--strictPort` and the ephemeral port reduce the risk but do not meet either credited mechanism. Mechanism (a) needs readiness taken from the child's output. Mechanism (b) needs a race against child exit.

The cited material therefore shows the offending-step assertion clause unmet, and the dissent's pass verdict does not refute the majority's reason.

Label and SceneLayer take NodeProps, whose props are all optional, and the template passes layoutId and children, which exist. The bootstrap tsconfig.app.json enables noUnusedLocals, noUnusedParameters and verbatimModuleSyntax; the templates use import type correctly and have no unused locals. entities.ts only exports entity, and <slug> appears only inside a string literal. The bootstrap's own starter presentation uses the same import shapes and field names against the same kit, and its registry entry imports './starter/Talk' correctly. The inspect template (bootstrap/scripts/inspect-presentation.mjs) imports only node built-ins and playwright, and it is not in the tsconfig include of src, so it has no relative imports to resolve. The remaining risk is that no test builds the presentation templates, but the trace finds no unmet clause.

votes.rationale: Readiness comes from HTTP polling of `http://127.0.0.1:${port}/`, not from the child's own announcement of its address. The only ownership check is `previewAlive(child)`, sampled at the top of each polling iteration, so the child's exit is not raced against readiness. A stale server on the port (for instance one bound after freePort releases it, or a user-supplied --port) can answer the fetch before the child's exit is observed. `--strictPort` and the ephemeral port reduce the risk but do not meet either credited mechanism. Mechanism (a) needs readiness taken from the child's output. Mechanism (b) needs a race against child exit.

first_results.rationale: The verifier code meets the requirement. renderRoutes listens for console messages of type 'error' (verify.mjs:116) and for 'pageerror' (verify.mjs:117). Each listener records activeIndex, which is set before each ArrowRight (line 126). After stepping, the first recorded error is thrown as `${slug} step ${index}: message` (line 133), and run() turns that into `FAIL [render]` with exit code 1 (lines 158-164). The review guidance also requires a representative browser-error test that asserts a non-zero exit and the offending step. In the 'runtime' fault, the test injects console.error only when payload.count === 3 (verify.e2e.test.ts:16). steps.tsx:19 sets count = index + 1, so the offending step is step 2. E2E-002 only asserts the loose regex /step [0-9]/ (test line 54). That regex accepts any single-digit step, including a wrong 'step 0' or 'step 8', so the test never checks that the offending step is the one reported. The executable-evidence clause is therefore unmet. Judge B's reason holds and decides the criterion. Judges A and C each describe the source and the test accurately. However, both treat /step [0-9]/ as proof that the offending step is reported, and that line does not check which step is reported, so their pass does not satisfy the guidance's requirement to assert the offending step.

first_results.rationale: The verifier's mechanism is sound. The step count must be a positive integer (verify.mjs:123-124), so a missing, zero, or non-numeric data-step-count throws 'rendered no steps' instead of stepping through nothing and passing. Each transition waits for Number(data-step-index) === expected, where expected starts at 1 (lines 125-129). first_results.rationale: I agree with judges A and B. All four copies spawn Vite's own binary with process.execPath, not through an npm or npx wrapper. The child they track is therefore the preview server itself. In verify, the preview is created in renderRoutes, and readiness, chromium.launch, and every route check all sit inside one try whose finally runs `await browser?.close(); await stopPreview()`. stopPreview sends SIGTERM to the process group and awaits the child's 'exit' event, capped at 3s, and only then escalates to SIGKILL. SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers also call stopPreview. In inspect, the spawn, readiness, browser launch, and every capture sit inside run()'s try, and its finally calls stopPreview. That function sends SIGTERM, awaits 'exit' (capped at 2s), then SIGKILL. Success, a failing check, a browser launch failure, and a later thrown error therefore all pass through the same awaited cleanup. The template copies are identical apart from the removed sample check, and the contract test enforces that. Judge C's reason does not decide the requirement. The SIGKILL without a second await is reached only when the server ignores SIGTERM for 2–3s. That is a hypothetical hang the candidate does not produce, not one of the named exit paths. On every named path the server is terminated and its exit awaited. The integration test also confirms that the port is refused after inspect exits.

results.rationale: I agree with judges A and B. All four copies spawn Vite's own binary with process.execPath, not through an npm or npx wrapper. The child they track is therefore the preview server itself. In verify, the preview is created in renderRoutes, and readiness, chromium.launch, and every route check all sit inside one try whose finally runs `await browser?.close(); await stopPreview()`. stopPreview sends SIGTERM to the process group and awaits the child's 'exit' event, capped at 3s, and only then escalates to SIGKILL. SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers also call stopPreview. In inspect, the spawn, readiness, browser launch, and every capture sit inside run()'s try, and its finally calls stopPreview. That function sends SIGTERM, awaits 'exit' (capped at 2s), then SIGKILL. Success, a failing check, a browser launch failure, and a later thrown error therefore all pass through the same awaited cleanup. The template copies are identical apart from the removed sample check, and the contract test enforces that. Judge C's reason does not decide the requirement. The SIGKILL without a second await is reached only when the server ignores SIGTERM for 2–3s. That is a hypothetical hang the candidate does not produce, not one of the named exit paths. On every named path the server is terminated and its exit awaited. The integration test also confirms that the port is refused after inspect exits.

results.rationale: All three clauses are met. Both template scripts are quoted in full so the auditor can check every line. (1) Target from an argument, or every registered route. The template verify reads src/presentations/index.ts. parsePresentationRoutes collects every `slug:` entry, not only the first, and fails if there are none. renderRoutes then loops `for (const route of routes)` and visits each one. The template inspect's parseArgs takes a required positional slug and rejects a missing or malformed one with a usage error. (2) Clear non-zero rejection of an unregistered slug. In the bootstrap main.tsx, the Router renders <Landing /> when presentationForPath finds no entry. Landing renders `<main data-host-landing>` and has no [data-presentation-root]. Inspect waits for [data-presentation-root] with a bounded 5000 ms limit. It catches that timeout and throws the explicit error `Unknown presentation slug or page failed to render: <slug>`. run() catches the error, prints `FAIL [inspect] ...` and returns 1, which becomes process.exitCode. So the landing fallback is never accepted: the script stops with a named, non-zero failure, not a generic timeout. Verify also refuses a step count below 1 (`rendered no steps`). (3) No sample-specific content. The full template verify (lines 1-157) has no sample-outline import, no checkSample, and no sample titles, captions or slug. compareOutline is a generic helper with no expected data. The full template inspect (lines 1-188) has only generic defaults: 1440x900 viewport, 1200 ms settle, and .presentation-inspection/<slug> output. Neither file contains the how-to-make-a-presentation route or any sample text. Why the other panel votes do not change this: - Judge C fails the criterion because inspect detects an unregistered slug through a browser timeout instead of a registry lookup. The requirement does not ask for a registry lookup. It asks that the slug be rejected with a clear non-zero failure, "rather than timing out or accepting the landing-page fallback". Lines 156-157 and 184 show the bounded wait is turned into an explicit `Unknown presentation slug` error with exit code 1. That is not a hang, not a bare timeout, and not acceptance of the fallback, so C's reason does not show any clause unmet. - Judges A and B both reach pass on the same mechanism.

results.rationale: Only three delivered tests start a browser: - tests/e2e/verify.e2e.test.ts - tests/integration/inspect-presentation.int.test.ts - tests/integration/bootstrap-template.int.test.ts All three are quoted in full. None of them calls setTimeout, waitForTimeout, a sleep or a delay before an assertion, and none treats an instant read as a wait. - The E2E test runs `npm run verify` with spawnSync, which blocks until the process exits, then asserts on status and output. - The two integration tests await a run() promise that resolves only on the child's 'exit' event (inspect int lines 78-87, bootstrap int lines 11-20), then assert. - The port checks (portIsFree, expectConnectionRefused) resolve on actual socket connect or error events, not on a timer. - The one time-based call, AbortSignal.timeout(2000) on the foreign-server fetch, is a request deadline, not a sleep before an assertion. The remaining tests are jsdom unit tests (vite.config.ts sets environment 'jsdom'). Their imports show only vitest, @testing-library/react, node fs/path and project modules, with no Playwright or browser driver, so they do not drive a browser. Why the other panel votes do not change this: - Judge C fails the criterion because the scripts these tests call use page.waitForTimeout (the inspect --settle value and verify's 650 ms). Those calls are in scripts/*.mjs, not in the tests. The criterion judges the delivered automated tests that drive a browser. Their waits, quoted here, are on process exit and observable socket state. The script-internal delays belong to the script-level criteria, so C's reason does not decide this one. - Judges A and B both reach pass on the same evidence.

result.rationale: All three clauses are met. Both template scripts are quoted in full so the auditor can check every line. (1) Target from an argument, or every registered route. The template verify reads src/presentations/index.ts. parsePresentationRoutes collects every `slug:` entry, not only the first, and fails if there are none. renderRoutes then loops `for (const route of routes)` and visits each one. The template inspect's parseArgs takes a required positional slug and rejects a missing or malformed one with a usage error. (2) Clear non-zero rejection of an unregistered slug. In the bootstrap main.tsx, the Router renders <Landing /> when presentationForPath finds no entry. Landing renders `<main data-host-landing>` and has no [data-presentation-root]. Inspect waits for [data-presentation-root] with a bounded 5000 ms limit. It catches that timeout and throws the explicit error `Unknown presentation slug or page failed to render: <slug>`. run() catches the error, prints `FAIL [inspect] ...` and returns 1, which becomes process.exitCode. So the landing fallback is never accepted: the script stops with a named, non-zero failure, not a generic timeout. Verify also refuses a step count below 1 (`rendered no steps`). (3) No sample-specific content. The full template verify (lines 1-157) has no sample-outline import, no checkSample, and no sample titles, captions or slug. compareOutline is a generic helper with no expected data. The full template inspect (lines 1-188) has only generic defaults: 1440x900 viewport, 1200 ms settle, and .presentation-inspection/<slug> output. Neither file contains the how-to-make-a-presentation route or any sample text. Why the other panel votes do not change this: - Judge C fails the criterion because inspect detects an unregistered slug through a browser timeout instead of a registry lookup. The requirement does not ask for a registry lookup. It asks that the slug be rejected with a clear non-zero failure, "rather than timing out or accepting the landing-page fallback".
